q.intro.text: Three fourths of a pan of brownies is frosted. Maya eats two thirds of the frosted part.

q.ask.text: How much of the whole pan does Maya eat?

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s1.text: The frosted part is cut into three equal rows. One row is one third of the frosted part.

e.s2.text: Maya eats two of the three rows: two thirds of the three fourths.

e.s3.text: Run the cuts on through the whole pan: twelve equal cells. Maya's part is six of them, six twelfths of the pan.

e.s4.text: Two thirds times three fourths is six twelfths. Rows times columns on top; all the cells of one pan underneath.

e.why.text: Quick check: why is twelve the bottom number?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. The bottom number counts the equal cells of one whole pan: three rows times four columns.

e.w-rule.text: The rule is right, but it has a reason: the cuts make three times four, twelve equal cells in the whole pan.

e.w-part.text: The frosted part has only nine cells. Twelve counts the whole pan.

t.intro.text: Now two fifths of a pan is left. Sam packs three fourths of what is left for lunch. The first two steps are done for you.

t.count.text: The cuts run on through the whole pan. What fraction of the whole pan does Sam pack?

t.fill.text: Fill in the top and the bottom box.

t.c-ok.text: Yes: six of the twenty cells of the whole pan, six twentieths.

t.c-part.text: Three fourths is the part of the leftover. Against the whole pan there are twenty cells, and six are packed.

t.c-add.text: That adds the cells of both fractions. Only the cells in both count: three rows times two columns.

t.c-other.text: Count the small cells: how many are packed, and how many are in the whole pan?

t.write.text: Tap the chips to write it as one equation.

t.w-ok.text: Yes: three fourths times two fifths is six twentieths. Of means times.

t.w-add.text: That adds or takes away. Sam packs a part of the leftover: that is times.

t.w-other.text: Use the two fractions of the story and the sign for of.

t.size.text: Is Sam's lunch more or less than the two fifths of a pan that was left?

t.s-ok.text: Right: three fourths is less than one, so Sam packs less than all of the leftover. Six twentieths is less than eight twentieths.

t.s-no.text: Look at the pan: the packed cells are only part of the leftover. Three fourths is less than one, so the product is less than two fifths.

t.simple.text: Six twentieths is three tenths: the same amount in simplest form.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked six twelfths, and you were right. Now you can show why.

t.cb-part.text: At the start you picked two thirds: that names the frosted part, not the whole pan. Maya eats six twelfths of the pan.

t.cb-add.text: At the start you picked one and five twelfths: that adds the fractions. Maya eats six twelfths of the pan, less than the frosted part.

p.intro.text: Riley says: multiplying always makes a number bigger, so two thirds times three fourths is more than three fourths.

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument and see where it leads.

p.prove.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Two thirds times three fourths means two thirds of the frosted three fourths,

p.c2.text: and two of three equal rows is less than all three rows,

p.c3.text: so two thirds times three fourths, six twelfths, is less than three fourths, nine twelfths.

p.x-bigger.text: That is Riley's idea, the one being tested. Multiplying by a number less than one makes it smaller.

p.x-examples.text: One example is not a reason: a reason must say why it works for every number.

p.x-shrink.text: Careful: five fourths times three fourths is more than three fourths. It depends on the factor being less than one.

p.x-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line.

p.done.text: That's a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the picture backs every one. Multiplying by a fraction less than one makes a number smaller.
